A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VisualPrompter, and their text, tables and figures support reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 includes readable Appendices A-M.

before.justification: V1 reports original DSG/TIFA evaluations, CLIP and aesthetic scores, component ablations, human preferences and generation examples.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds generator evaluations, repeated-seed results, independent-evaluator checks and further human comparisons.

M1.justification: The core SERE/TSPO procedure remains unchanged: identify missing concepts, expand them, reconstruct prompts and decorate them. Appendix I adds a limited adaptation using ControlNet, skeletal conditioning and VLM feedback on skeleton-image alignment. The newly supplied prompt templates primarily document the existing procedure.

E1.justification: The DSG/TIFA benchmarks and existing online-generator demonstrations are retained. Appendices I and K extend coverage to skeleton-conditioned generation, additional complex-scene prompts and Chinese-language generation with Kolors. These introduce new input conditions and language coverage, although their evidence is qualitative.

E2.justification: V1's human study compares optimized prompts only against original prompts; v2 Table 11 additionally compares VisualPrompter against NeuroPrompts, Promptist and BeautifulPrompt. Tables 6 and 10 introduce Qwen3-32B as a comparator, distinct from the retained Qwen2 comparisons. The principal benchmark comparator set otherwise remains unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 adds Janus-Pro to the quantitative generator settings, reevaluates results with Llama-3.2-11B-Vision instead of the feedback VLM, and introduces end-to-end timing and competitor-based human evaluations. These substantially extend the evaluation design. The original benchmark sizes, core metrics and stated 10-annotator/50-sample study settings are retained.

E4.justification: The existing component and decorator ablations are retained. V2 adds seed sensitivity, independent-evaluator robustness, inference-time measurements, explicit failure cases and case studies of complex prompts, Chinese inputs and skeletal conditioning. These examine several limitations and robustness questions untested in the supplied v1.

E5.justification: Appendix H and Table 10 newly report five-seed means and standard deviations for three approaches using SD v1.5 and Flux-dev on DSG. V1 provides no corresponding repeated-run uncertainty reporting. This is a limited statistical addition; it does not establish an increase from a previously specified run count or provide uncertainty throughout the main results.

E6.justification: The retained three-generator semantic, CLIP, aesthetic and component-ablation scores remain unchanged. V2 adds substantial results, including Janus-Pro semantic scores of 82.6 on DSG and 93.7 on TIFA, independent-judge scores, timing and seed summaries. Table 11 newly shows semantic preference for VisualPrompter but frequent aesthetic preference for competitors. Changed CLIP averages reflect adding Janus-Pro, not same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The appendix explanation of DSG construction elaborates the existing concept-question dependency mechanism, and its proportion-of-yes-responses score restates the definition already given in v1.

C1.justification: V2 removes v1's explicit claim to be the first to exploit VLM visual feedback for T2I prompt engineering. It emphasizes atomic semantic preservation more prominently, while retaining the central training-free optimization, semantic-alignment, state-of-the-art performance and broad compatibility claims.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's brief hallucination and latency limitations, v2 discusses multi-object failures, missed VLM errors, long-prompt constraints, evaluator bias, seed stability and multilingual applicability. It also changes the explanation of NeuroPrompts' poor CLIP scores from randomly selected keyword conflicts to restricted keyword diversity. These are substantive additions and revisions to interpretation.

D1.justification: V2 supplies DSG construction details, prompt templates, invalid-output regeneration instructions, keyword examples and selection counts, model-size information, and a code-repository link. Appendix J documents the human-study interface, hidden optimized prompts and randomized image positions. These substantially improve documentation, although v1's explicit disclosure of random NeuroPrompts keyword selection disappears.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting extensions such as Janus-Pro and ControlNet, removes several older references, and drops the first-use claim for VLM feedback. Related-work discussion is condensed, but its central positioning against aesthetic-focused prompt engineering remains.

P1.justification: The overview, contributions and conclusion are substantially rewritten, while related-work and metric explanations are condensed. Detailed result discussion and limitations are reorganized into appendices alongside expanded procedural explanations and explicit cross-references. The title also gains 'Semantic-Aware'.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a single-column conference layout, replaces Figure 1 examples, redraws the pipeline and shortens Figure 3. It introduces a combined benchmark summary and relocates retained detailed results to appendix tables. New procedural diagrams, case-study figures, and timing, uncertainty, human-comparison and evaluator tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: The supplied v1 lacks its referenced procedural supplements and uses its feedback VLM for semantic benchmark evaluation. V2 adds concrete prompt templates, an independent Llama-Vision evaluation, direct human comparisons against competitors and five-seed summaries. These substantially strengthen reproducibility and evidential credibility. New human results reveal an aesthetic tradeoff, and some broad superiority language remains, but the validation and documentation gains clearly outweigh these limitations.
